questions.question: In this passage, how does Tacitus create a lively portrait of Otho?
questions.instruction: You should refer both to the content and to the language of the passage.
passage: neque erat Galbae ignota Othonis ac Titi Vinii amicitia; et rumoribus nihil silentio
transmittentium, quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho, gener ac socer destinabantur.
credo et rei publicae curam subisse, frustra a Nerone translatae si apud Othonem
relinqueretur. namque Otho pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat,
gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus. eoque Poppaeam Sabinam, principale scortum,
ut apud conscium libidinum deposuerat, donec Octaviam uxorem amoliretur. mox
suspectum in eadem Poppaea in provinciam Lusitaniam specie legationis seposuit.
Otho comiter administrata provincia primus in partes transgressus nec segnis et, donec
bellum fuit, inter praesentes splendidissimus, spem adoptionis statim conceptam acrius
in dies rapiebat, faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut similem.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively description of Otho by detailing the responses elicited by the possibility of his succession.
He writes,
‘et rumoribus nihil silentio transmittentium, quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho, gener ac socer destinabantur,’
which translates to,

‘and in the gossip of the people, who let nothing pass by in silence, Otho was being marked out as the son-in-law and Vinius the father-in-law, because Otho was a bachelor and Vinius had an unmarried daughter.’
Here,
the consonance of ‘m’ and ‘n’
mimics the impression of the people’s gossip, thus reflecting the animated response created by Otho.
Also, Tacitus asserts,
‘credo et rei publicae curam subisse, frustra a Nerone translatae si apud Othonem relinqueretur,’
meaning,
‘I believe that concern for the state influenced Galba, as it would have been removed from Nero in vain if it were to be left in the hands of Otho.’
The alliteration of ‘c’
places further emphasis on Tacitus’ remark, and the argument that Otho can be likened to Nero gives the impression that he is a man of excess.
Tacitus also creates a lively portrait of Otho by revealing his immorality.
He writes,
‘namque Otho pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat, gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus,’
which means,
‘for Otho had spent his boyhood negligently, his youth under no restraints, being pleasing to Nero as an imitation of his lust,’
and here
the balanced phrasing of ‘pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam’ (with the nouns followed by adverbs)
creates the impression that Otho’s recklessness has endured throughout his life, without ever changing.
In addition, Tacitus foregrounds Otho’s corruption in,
‘eoque Poppaeam Sabinam, principale scortum, ut apud conscium libidinum deposuerat, donec Octaviam uxorem amolietur,’
which translates to,
‘and for that Nero left with him, as into the keeping of one who was aware of his lusts, Poppaea Sabina, the imperial whore, until he could get rid of his wife Octavia.’
The use of such objectifying language in describing this action, such as ‘principale scortum’ and ‘amolietur’,
creates a lively portrait of Otho by revealing him as a man who condones and is complicit in the misogynistic treatment of women.
Additionally, Tacitus’ description of Otho is made more lively by his revelation of Otho’s positive attributes and the support he garnered.
He writes,
‘Otho comiter administrata provincia primus in partes transgressus nec segnis et, donec bellum fuit, inter praesentes splendidissimus,’
which means,

‘after he had administered the province graciously, Otho was the first to join Galba’s party, and he was not inactive, and, for as long as the war last, he was the most brilliant among his immediate supporters.’
Tacitus’ use of such positive language in reference to Otho, with the superlative of ‘splendidissimus’,
depicts Otho as a hard-working and exceptional man.
Furthermore, this is also shown when Tacitus writes,
‘spem adoptionis statim conceptam acrius in dies rapiebat,’
meaning,
‘he conceived at once the hope for the adoption, and was grasping for it more eagerly each day.’
Here,
the language of immediacy and fervour which Tacitus utilises, such as, ‘statim,’ ‘acrius,’ and ‘rapiebat’,
highlights Otho’s activity and passion in striving for his ambition of the adoption.
Otho’s portrait is also made lively by Tacitus’ reference to his supporters,
in,
‘faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut similem,’
which translates to,
‘with the majority of the soldiers favouring him, and Nero’s court inclined to him as being like Nero.’
The liveliness here is conveyed in the hyperbaton of ‘prona’ and ‘aula’,
as this enables these words to surround ‘eum’ in order to imitate the support which enveloped Otho.
Thus, Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by detailing this simultaneously corrupt yet extraordinary man, and the reactions to him.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). The point about how Otho spent his boyhood and youth negligently is excellent: a good quote with accurate translation. Then a literary device is identified (balanced phrasing), and the effect of this balance is well developed. There is a wide range of points which covers the entirety of the passage. The question is directly answered by an appropriate selection of evidence.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by linking him to Titus Vinius, a man who Tacitus has made clear that people hated him.
“Othonis ac Titi Vinii amicitia”
(the friendship of Otho and Titus Vinius)
is also shown to be well known as
“gener ac socer destinabanter”
(they were called son-in-law and father-in-law)
even though
“caelebs Otho”
(Otho was single)
This variatio
mirrors the many different ways Otho and Titus are linked together
and the fact Otho is so close to a hated man makes him more interesting.
Otho’s history with Nero also makes him interesting.
Tacitus remarks on how Otho
“pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat”
(spent his boyhood carelessly, adolescense recklessly)
and
the asyndeton
helps to show just how quickly it went by.
Otho is also said to
“Neroni aemulatione luxus”
(copy the luxury of Nero)
which seemed to include
“Poppaean Sabinam, principale scortum”
(Poppaea Sabina, the imperial whore)
The juxtaposition of “principale scortum”
is really meant to demean Poppaea by combining such a high class title with a vulgar word and that fact that it is neuter objectifys her into something to be passed around.
But the fact Otho is trusted with her shows Nero’s fondness of him until he is
“suspectum in eadem Poppaea”
(suspected in the case of the same Poppea)
. Otho is
“specie legationis seposuit”
(exiled under the cover of a legate)
which shows that Nero still cared about Otho’s reputation.
Otho’s time during and after Lusitania adds to the lively portrait of Otho.
Otho
“comiter administrata provincia”
(governs the province in a friendly way)
and
“nec segnis et, donec bellum fuit”
(is not lazy, as long as there is war)
The brevitas of the second part of the statement
seems to undermine the compliment given in the first half.
Otho also seems obsessed with being adopted by Galba as he wanted it
“statim conceptam”
(as soon as it was concieved)
and
“acrius in dies rapiebat”
(was wanting it more sharply everyday)
. Otho is
“faventibus plerisque militum”
(favoured by very many soldiers)
which is very useful to Otho later
and is seen as
“similem”
(similar)
to Nero by his palace and as it was placed at
a point of emphasis
, the similarities between Nero and Otho must be important.

exemplars.commentary: There is good engagement here (Level 4) showing some points which however are not always developed. The point about gener ac socer is good, but the literary device of variation is not sufficiently pointed out or explained. The range of points is also a little limited – more material is needed if such responses are to reach the higher levels. The point about Otho being similem is relevant (as is the note about the emphatic placement of the adjective), but there is limitation in the amount of Latin and context/quotation offered.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by describing his
‘pueritiam incuriose’
(indifferent childhood)
the emotive use of the word ‘incuriose’ (indifferent)
shows in which ways he was similar to Nero and very different from Galba.
He spent some of his youth with Nero emulting in excess with his lusts. As we know what Nero was like this helps us better understand what Otho will be like.
This is further the case when it is stated
‘prona in eum pala Neronis ut similem’
(The palace was bias to him as he was similar to Nero)
The emphatic posistion of ‘similem’ (similar)
further highlights just how similar they both were.
Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by highlighting the vices of him.
He lusted for Poppaea Sabina the
‘principale scortum’
(cheif whore)
which is what lead to him being exiled to Lustiania by Nero.
However, to contrast this Tacitus then portrays the good things in which Otho had done. For example, upon being exiled he was not inactive an
‘bellum fuit, inter praesentes splendidissimus’
(when in war, he was in as one of the most distinguished)
Tacitus creates a lively portrait by talking about Otho’s companions.
Not only does he talk about Nero and Poppaea as the people he chooses to surround himself with but he also talks about the close relationship he has with Titus Vinius even describing them as
‘quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho’
(father-in-law and son in law and Vinius had an unmarried daughter and Otho was a bachelor)
. This is the rumour that was spread by the people.
This creates a lively portrait as we see how others perceive him.
Furthermore, by stating who he associates with we can perhaps judge his character.

exemplars.commentary: There is some engagement in this response (Level 3). Noticeably, the response is on the short side and this lack of range of points will inevitably lead to a lower level. The response begins with some erroneous translation regarding the ‘indifferent childhood’. The point about the court of Nero being similar to Otho is a good quote/translation, but the emphatic position is not properly explained and developed. The point about the principale scortum also shows just some engagement (without a fuller quote or context however which again leads towards a lower level).
